priority_actions.title: Priority actions
priority_actions.intro_source: Recommended actions to improve your IISRI rating, ordered by severity and priority

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Broad data collection tied to your identity when signed in. Once you log into a Google Account, most of what you do across Search, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, and other services gets stored with your personal profile — searches, videos watched, purchase activity, communications, and even uploaded media. This makes it hard to use Google services without accumulating a detailed history linked to you.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Tracking even when signed out. Google says it collects and stores data using unique identifiers tied to your browser, app, or device even when you're not signed in. So not having an account doesn't necessarily mean you're anonymous — your activity can still be profiled and linked to your device.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Incognito mode doesn't fully shield you. The policy explicitly notes that third-party sites and apps using Google services (ads, analytics, embedded content) still share information with Google even when you're in Chrome Incognito mode. Users expecting full privacy in private browsing may be surprised.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Persistent cross-device and cross-service tracking. Google may use data collected across services and devices — and if you use third-party sites with Google ads or analytics, that activity may be associated with your personal information. This can be hard to mentally model or fully control.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Location data can be inferred in multiple ways. Even if one location setting is off, Google may use IP address, sensor data, Wi-Fi access points, cell towers, and nearby Bluetooth devices to determine location. This makes it hard to truly opt out of location inference.

actions.title: Security
actions.action_required_source: Automated analysis of your content. Google uses automated systems to analyze your content for personalization, spam, malware, and illegal content detection. That means your emails, documents, and photos may be scanned by algorithms, even if humans aren't reading them.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Data sharing with domain administrators. If you use Google services through work or school, your administrator and resellers may access, retain, or even delete your data and restrict your privacy controls. You may have little say over this.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Data sharing for legal and business reasons. Google can share personal information in response to government requests or legal process, to enforce terms, or during a merger or acquisition. This means your data could end up with another company under a different privacy policy.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Vague retention periods. The policy says some data is kept "until you delete your account," some is retained longer for "legitimate business or legal purposes," and deletion from backups may be delayed. It's hard to know exactly how long your data sticks around.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Data stored and processed globally. Your information may be processed on servers outside your country, where data protection laws might be weaker. Google says it applies the same protections everywhere, but oversight and enforcement may vary by jurisdiction.

actions.title: Security
actions.action_required_source: Changes to the policy without your explicit consent (for non-right-reducing changes). Google says it won't reduce your rights without explicit consent, but other changes can be made unilaterally, with only "prominent notice" for significant ones. You may miss updates buried in notifications.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Many controls require manual effort and can be buried. While Google offers extensive privacy controls, they're spread across Privacy Checkup, My Activity, Dashboard, ad settings, and device settings. Keeping on top of all of them is a real burden for an average user.

actions.title: Security
actions.action_required_source: Public exposure through normal use. Comments, reviews, shared endorsements, and even your name and photo can appear publicly or in ads alongside your activity. If you don't actively change defaults, you may be more visible than you expect.

actions.title: Reset Compromised Credentials
actions.action_required_source: Force password reset for 15879 affected accounts. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users.
actions.why_this_matters_source: Leaked credentials could allow unauthorized access to your systems.

actions.title: Enhance DMARC Policy to "Quarantine"
actions.action_required_source: Upgrade DMARC policy from monitoring (p=none) to quarantine (p=quarantine) to actively protect against email spoofing.
actions.why_this_matters_source: Prevents attackers from impersonating your domain in phishing attacks.

remediation_impact.narrative_source: 224 active issues were identified (13 privacy issues, 211 vulnerability findings, 15879 exposed credentials). Completing the recommended actions is expected to recover up to 194 points, moving the score from 86 to 280 out of 360. This assumes every vulnerability finding is fixed and confirmed by a fresh scan, the reported privacy issues are remediated in the privacy policy and every exposed credential is reset. Vulnerability fixes only affect the rating after the next scan, so the projected score is conditional on that rescan.

findings.rationale_source: A HIGH severity certificate trust vulnerability (e.g., misissued, expired, or self-signed certificate in a trust chain) can enable man-in-the-middle attacks or spoofing, leading to credential theft or data interception. However, exploitation requires an attacker to be in a privileged network position (e.g., on-path) and for users or systems to interact with the malicious endpoint. Without evidence of active exploitation or a widespread, known-bad CA compromise, the likelihood is moderate but not imminent.

The use of deprecated ciphers like 3DES and IDEA is a known weakness that degrades overall cryptographic security. While not an immediate, direct path to a breach, it lowers the security posture and could be leveraged as part of a broader attack chain, especially if combined with other vulnerabilities. The risk is present but not imminent without active exploitation or additional context.

A medium-severity certificate expiration is a reliability and availability issue, not a direct confidentiality or integrity flaw. It can lead to service disruption, degraded trust, and potential man-in-the-middle opportunities if combined with other weaknesses, but does not directly cause a data breach on its own.

An expired certificate (cert_notAfter) is a medium-severity misconfiguration that disrupts service availability and trust, creating an opportunity for man-in-the-middle attacks or service impersonation. However, without evidence of active exploitation or a specific attack chain leveraging this flaw, the direct likelihood of a full breach remains low. The risk is contingent on an attacker being in a position to intercept traffic and the absence of other protective controls.

BEAST is a known cryptographic attack against CBC mode in TLS 1.0 and earlier. While a MEDIUM severity finding, modern clients and servers have implemented mitigations, and TLS 1.0 is largely deprecated. Direct exploitation requires a man-in-the-middle position and specific conditions, making a full breach unlikely in a generic context without confirmed vulnerable configurations or active adversarial presence.

A misconfigured or missing Content-Security-Policy (CSP) is a common security weakness that increases the risk of client-side attacks like XSS. However, exploitation requires a separate, exploitable vulnerability (e.g., an XSS flaw) to be present in the application. The MEDIUM severity reflects this indirect but significant enabling role. Without evidence of an active XSS vector, the direct breach likelihood remains low but non-zero.

BREACH is a side-channel attack requiring specific conditions (HTTP compression, attacker-in-the-middle, repeated requests) to extract secrets from encrypted traffic. While a real vulnerability, successful exploitation is non-trivial and depends on attacker positioning and target application behavior, making a direct breach unlikely in a generic scenario.

TLS 1.0 is a deprecated protocol with known cryptographic weaknesses (e.g., BEAST). While it increases the risk of information disclosure if an attacker is in a position to perform a man-in-the-middle attack, exploitation requires a specific, active adversary on the network path. It is not a direct, remotely exploitable vulnerability leading to system compromise. The likelihood of this single finding directly causing a breach is very low.

TLS 1.1 is a deprecated protocol with known cryptographic weaknesses, but exploitation requires a man-in-the-middle position and is not directly actionable for initial access. Modern clients and servers typically negotiate stronger protocols, making successful exploitation of this specific finding for a full breach highly unlikely in a generic context.

A LOW severity cipher list misconfiguration, while a technical weakness, does not directly enable a breach. It typically requires an attacker to already be in a privileged position to exploit (e.g., man-in-the-middle). Without active exploitation or additional critical flaws, the direct likelihood of a breach is minimal.

TLS session ticket vulnerabilities (LOW severity) typically involve theoretical weaknesses like ticket predictability or lack of perfect forward secrecy. They require a man-in-the-middle position and specific conditions to exploit, are not commonly targeted, and do not directly lead to a breach without other significant flaws or attacker access.

HSTS is a security enhancement, not a vulnerability. Its absence or misconfiguration (LOW severity) does not directly enable a breach. It only protects against specific, targeted SSL/TLS downgrade attacks, which are not common initial intrusion vectors. The likelihood of a breach stemming solely from this finding is negligible.

SWEET32 is a cryptographic vulnerability in legacy 64-bit block ciphers like 3DES and Blowfish. While a theoretical attack exists, it requires capturing massive amounts of encrypted data (hundreds of gigabytes) from a single session, which is an unrealistic scenario for most modern, generic applications. Modern systems and protocols have largely deprecated or mitigated these weak ciphers. The LOW severity reflects the impractical attack requirements and widespread mitigations, making direct breach from this flaw highly unlikely.

BEAST is a legacy client-side attack against TLS 1.0 and early implementations of TLS 1.1. Modern browsers and servers have implemented effective mitigations for over a decade. The vulnerability requires a man-in-the-middle position and significant effort to exploit, and TLS 1.0/1.1 are widely deprecated and disabled. Therefore, the realistic likelihood of this directly leading to a breach is negligible.

LUCKY13 is a low-severity cryptographic timing side-channel attack against TLS/SSL implementations. It requires a specific, controlled environment to exploit, is difficult to execute reliably over a network, and modern systems have mitigations. The direct breach likelihood from this finding alone is negligible.

results.summary_source: The security scan identified only informational findings related to SMTP service detection and command enumeration on the host imap.gmail.com. No vulnerabilities of critical, high, medium, or low severity were discovered. These findings are typical of standard network reconnaissance and do not indicate any immediate security risk. The overall security posture appears strong, but continued monitoring and adherence to best practices are recommended.
recommendations_source: Ensure SMTP services are properly secured with authentication and encryption (TLS) to prevent unauthorized access and data interception.
Regularly review and restrict SMTP command capabilities to only those necessary for business operations.
Monitor SMTP logs for unusual activity and consider rate limiting to mitigate abuse.

findings.title: SMTP Service Detection on Port 25
findings.description: The scan detected an SMTP service listening on port 25. SMTP is used for email transmission and is a common service that may be targeted for spam relay or phishing if misconfigured.
findings.impact: If the SMTP service is misconfigured, it could be abused for spam or phishing, potentially damaging the organization's reputation and leading to blacklisting.
findings.remediation: 1. Ensure SMTP authentication is required for sending emails. 2. Implement TLS encryption for SMTP connections. 3. Restrict relay permissions to authorized networks only. 4. Regularly update and patch the SMTP server software.

findings.title: SMTP Service Detection on Port 587
findings.description: The scan detected an SMTP service listening on port 587, which is typically used for email submission with authentication. This is a standard configuration for secure email submission.
findings.impact: No immediate impact, but if authentication is not enforced, it could be exploited for unauthorized email sending.
findings.remediation: 1. Enforce authentication on port 587. 2. Require TLS encryption (STARTTLS). 3. Monitor for abuse and implement rate limiting.

findings.title: SMTP Commands Enumeration
findings.description: The scan enumerated SMTP commands using EHLO and HELP, revealing the extended commands supported by the server. This information can be used by attackers to understand the server's capabilities.
findings.impact: Low risk, but detailed information about the SMTP server could aid in targeted attacks if not properly secured.
findings.remediation: 1. Disable unnecessary SMTP commands. 2. Ensure the server is configured to not disclose sensitive information in banners. 3. Keep the SMTP server software up to date.

results.summary_source: The security scan identified two informational findings related to SMTP service detection on smtp.gmail.com (ports 25 and 587). No actual vulnerabilities were discovered. These findings simply confirm the presence of standard email service ports, which is expected for a mail server. The overall security posture is not negatively impacted by these results.
recommendations_source: No immediate action required; these are informational findings only.
Ensure SMTP services are properly secured with authentication and encryption (e.g., TLS) if not already in place.
Regularly review exposed services to confirm they are intentionally public and necessary.

findings.title: SMTP Service Detection on Port 25
findings.description: The scan detected an SMTP service listening on port 25 of smtp.gmail.com. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used for sending and relaying email. This is an informational finding indicating the presence of a mail server, not a vulnerability.
findings.impact: No direct business impact. This is expected behavior for an email service provider. However, unauthenticated or unencrypted SMTP could be abused for spam if misconfigured, but this is a standard service.
findings.remediation: 1. Verify that SMTP on port 25 is configured to require authentication for relaying. 2. Ensure TLS encryption is enforced for email transmission. 3. Monitor for abuse and apply rate limiting as needed. 4. No action is required if this is an intentional public mail service.

findings.title: SMTP Service Detection on Port 587
findings.description: The scan detected an SMTP service listening on port 587 of smtp.gmail.com. Port 587 is typically used for email submission with authentication and encryption (STARTTLS). This is an informational finding, not a vulnerability.
findings.impact: No direct business impact. This is a standard and recommended port for email submission. It indicates the service supports secure email sending.
findings.remediation: 1. Confirm that port 587 enforces STARTTLS and authentication. 2. Ensure strong authentication mechanisms are in place. 3. Regularly update and patch the mail server software. 4. No action is required if this is an intentional public mail service.

scope_and_limitations.title: a. Scope and limitations
scope_and_limitations.intro: We cannot guarantee that a domain or organization is fully quantum-safe based on the results of this assessment because:
items: Post-quantum cryptography is an evolving field. Cryptographic standards, implementations, and the understanding of quantum computing capabilities continue to develop. Future advances may affect the security of algorithms considered secure today.

This is a non-invasive, external assessment. Unless an internal CyberRank agent is deployed, the scan evaluates only externally observable services and configurations. Internal systems, private networks, and services that are not externally accessible are outside the scope of this assessment.

post_quantum_readiness.title: b. Post-quantum readiness
post_quantum_readiness.intro: A domain can only be considered fully post-quantum ready if it:
items: Supports post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms for secure connections; and
Disables legacy TLS versions (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and TLS 1.2).
post_quantum_readiness.closing: Allowing legacy TLS versions enables clients to establish connections using classical cryptographic algorithms. If an attacker can force or negotiate the use of an older protocol version (a protocol downgrade), the connection may lose the protections provided by post-quantum cryptography.

c_methodology.title: Methodology and supply-chain aggregation
c_methodology.note: Generic methodology brief appended to the old PDF; values in its diagrams (e.g. Individual risk Low, Combined risk Medium) are illustrative, not Claude results.
c_methodology.headline_source: One rating for every vendor. One risk number for your whole supply chain.
c_methodology.lead_source: CYBERRANK turns externally observable evidence about an organisation into a single severity rating, a normalised risk score, and a combined risk that includes the vendors — and the vendors' vendors — behind it.

columns_source.title: The problem
columns_source.text: Attackers reach organisations through their suppliers. Existing tools don't add up: CVSS scores single technical flaws, questionnaires rely on self-reporting, and privacy, AI and quantum exposures have no common scale at all.

columns_source.title: The approach
columns_source.text: An ISO 31000-aligned model with four explicit steps, from observed weaknesses to supply-chain risk. Every step is reproducible and every number is comparable across organisations and portfolios.

columns_source.title: The regulatory fit
columns_source.text: Built for the obligations in DORA, NIS2, the GDPR and the AI Act, and aligned with ISO/IEC 27001, 27701 and 42001, NIST SP 800-53 and 800-161, PCI DSS and the NIST CSF.

steps_source.title: Observe
steps_source.text: Continuous external signals are collected without touching the organisation's systems.
steps_source.callout: Certified controls earn credits: ISO 27001, ISO 27701, SOC 2, ISAE 3402, PCI DSS. Optional questionnaires add a second, bounded evidence channel.
callout_emphasis: ISO 27001, ISO 27701, SOC 2, ISAE 3402, PCI DSS

steps_source.title: Rate
steps_source.text: Every organisation starts with a full point budget, split evenly between a security bucket and a privacy bucket. Weaknesses deduct capped demerits; certifications add capped credits.
steps_source.callout: The net score maps to the IISRI rating, AAA to D. The rating reflects the organisation's own posture only — a vendor's weakness never changes it.

steps_source.title: Score the risk
steps_source.text:
Likelihood = threat probability × weakness. Threat probability comes from sector, size and internet exposure; weakness comes from the rating.

Impact is one of four tiers you assign: Critical, High, Medium or Low.
steps_source.callout: Risk = normalised likelihood × impact, reported as a score and a band: Low, Medium, High or Critical.

steps_source.title: Combine
steps_source.text: Vendors and sub-vendors are discovered automatically and rated with the same pipeline. Their risks are folded into yours, attenuated by distance in the chain.
steps_source.callout: The combined risk shows the cascading exposure that your own rating cannot see.

c_methodology.scale_caption_source: Ten grades. Higher grades mean lower weakness values and therefore lower likelihood.

scale_ends_source.top: All controls adequate, appropriate and effective

supply_chain.headline_source: Your rating describes you. Your combined risk describes your supply chain.
supply_chain.text_source: Every vendor and sub-vendor is rated with the same pipeline as you are. A weak vendor never lowers your own rating — that stays attributable to your posture. But an exploited vendor can open an attack path into your systems, so the same weakness does enter your combined risk, attenuated by how far away it sits in the chain. The result is two complementary numbers. Read together, they show that an excellent rating does not certify a healthy supply chain.
supply_chain.formula_title_source: Combined risk — the "at least one adverse event" composition, applied recursively through the chain
supply_chain.formula: R(N) = 1 − (1 − o_N) · Π_{s ∈ suppliers(N)} ( 1 − R(s) / (f + d(s))² )
supply_chain.formula_explainer_source: Every supplier's effective risk R(s) already contains its own suppliers, so the chain unrolls from the outermost leaves inward. Each factor is one party's chance of not causing an incident; one minus the product is the chance that something, somewhere in the chain, goes wrong.

variables.text: A node's own individual risk score — from its rating, threat probability and impact tier.
A supplier's effective risk, computed the same way from its own suppliers. A leaf with no suppliers has R = o_N.
Hops from the centre: d(s) = d(N) + 1. Each supplier sits one step further out and is damped more.
The transmission fraction you configure. A larger f trusts distance more and shrinks every supplier's contribution.
Your combined risk: the formula evaluated at your own organisation A, the centre of the graph (d = 0).

impact_tiers.text: Failure immediately stops a critical service or causes a serious regulatory breach. DORA: critical.
Essential, but a temporary loss can be bridged with workarounds. DORA: important.
Supports normal operations; disruption means inconvenience. The default tier at onboarding.

reliance_points.title: Standards-grounded
reliance_points.text: ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 27001, 27701 and 42001, NIST SP 800-30 and 800-53, DORA and NIS2.

reliance_points.title: Certified operator
reliance_points.text: an independently audited ISO/IEC 27001 management system; ISO/IEC 42001 certification in progress.

reliance_points.title: Human in the loop
reliance_points.text: users report inaccuracies and appeal findings; feedback tunes detection confidence over time.

reliance_points.title: Honest about limits
reliance_points.text: vendor compromises are treated as independent, some detections are heuristic, and the continuous score is primary over the qualitative heat map.

supply_chain.closing_source: An organisation's own excellent rating does not certify its supply chain. Only the combined risk does.
supply_chain.dashboard_note_source: The dashboard shows, for you and every (sub-)vendor, six domains — Security, Privacy, Data leaks, Controls, AI, Quantum — plus the IISRI rating, the individual risk and the combined risk.

review_flags.text: Action 15 recommends moving DMARC from p=none, but the DMARC line prints an empty mode ("Enabled ( mode)").
IP reputation prints "Clean" while every abuse score is the sentinel -1 and ISP / country are blank.
Affected-asset labels mta, multisend are truncated host names (printed as is).
Cover band text for CC ("risks are being managed") differs from the CC meaning in Appendix A ("issues are being managed").
Scope rows for RSA and ECDHE print Risk "Low" ("covered by ML-KEM") with their count in the High column; the 30 High-risk headline equals those rows.
Organisation description ends with a stray token ("access. jij"); kept verbatim.
Headline "15879 Found" and action 14 ("15879 affected accounts") vs 5395 register rows; 587 rows are on other email domains, so the figure is neither rows nor organisation accounts.

The Last Valid Breach card says "This breach is used in the rating calculation" for an event marked "(Reported Inaccurate)". The 17-leak headline counts it with 16 historical records "not directly used in current scoring", yet the data-leak score is 0%.

Remediation counts 211 vulnerability findings; the finding cards hold 183 finding-asset memberships and the active scan 7 informational findings. 224 active issues = 13 + 211 excludes the 15879 credentials named in the same sentence.
Resourcing says the organisation has "a privacy function and a security function" but lists one role (Data Protection Officer), a privacy role.
Active scan of imap.gmail.com reports "5 findings" and lists "Detailed Findings (3)".

Field categories mix field keys (password, email) with breach data-class labels (Passwords, Email addresses) and variants (pass); 139 distinct categories are kept as printed. 2 rows list a password only under such a label, so a key-only password count misses them.
Every category prints "· 1 domain" while the findings cover 15 scopes (e.g. AES_128 — 15 findings).
